analysis.one_liner: Lets Oregon apply its universal health coverage laws to employer health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Oregon's health plan cover everyone died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1974 federal law (ERISA) generally stops states from regulating health coverage that employers provide directly. This short bill would carve out an exception for Oregon, allowing the state's Oregon Health Plan laws — employer coverage requirements, a high-risk pool, and cost controls — to apply to those employer plans, so Oregon could pursue universal coverage. It also would have let Oregon keep its own approach if Congress later passed national health reform.
analysis.who_benefits: Oregonians without health coverage, who would gain access under the Oregon Health Plan's phased-in employer coverage mandate; and workers whose employer plans would have to meet Oregon's minimum coverage standards. The state itself gains the legal authority to run its own universal coverage system.

how_it_helps.text: The bill exempts a list of Oregon laws — the high-risk insurance pool, employer coverage reforms, cost containment, and the phased-in employer mandate of the Oregon Health Plan — from ERISA's rule that federal law preempts state regulation of self-insured employer plans [S3].
It also includes a catch-all exemption for any Oregon law 'necessary to achieve universal coverage under the Oregon Health Plan,' giving the state room to complete its coverage expansion [S3].
Any Oregon tax on employers or health plans to fund coverage would have to be uniform and non-discriminatory, a constraint built into the exemption itself [S3].
Section 3 would have protected Oregon from being forced out of its own approach if Congress later enacted a national health reform law, until every other state had comparable coverage [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers in Oregon, who would face coverage requirements and possible assessments under the Oregon Health Plan laws the bill unshackles, and health insurers and self-insured employer plans, which would become subject to state regulation they are currently exempt from.

drawbacks.text: The bill would let one state impose employer coverage mandates and assessments on multistate employer plans, which employers argue creates a patchwork of differing state rules and administrative costs for companies operating across state lines [S3].

The Oregon Health Plan's employer mandate and uniform assessments shift the cost of covering the uninsured onto Oregon employers and their workers through premiums or taxes; the bill acknowledges this by conditioning its exemption on taxes being uniform and non-discriminatory [S3].
It applies only to Oregon, doing nothing for uninsured people elsewhere, and its narrow scope reflects how contested national health reform was at the time [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Oregonians, the benefit is potentially large: a path to universal coverage run by their own state. The costs fall on Oregon employers through mandated coverage and assessments, which can translate into lower wages or dropped plans if employers choose not to comply. The bill is a narrow legal fix — a one-state ERISA waiver — so it neither fixes the national employer-based insurance system nor creates a funding mechanism itself; it simply lets an already-enacted state plan operate.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee, then to a subcommittee in late December, and never came back out or reached the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on November 22, 1993, with Rep. Elizabeth Furse as the bill's other sponsor, during the peak of the national health reform debate [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S5].
On December 22, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, where no further action was recorded before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5] [S1].
It had only one cosponsor besides the sponsor and never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and insurers whose plans are shielded from state health regulation by ERISA are better off, since the exemption was never enacted and Oregon's Health Plan laws still cannot reach them. The bill's death also fits a broader pattern: after national health reform failed in 1994, no state got a comparable ERISA carve-out.

for.name: Rep. Ron Wyden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt Oregon's Health Plan laws from ERISA preemption.

for.name: Rep. Elizabeth Furse
for.role: Original cosponsor, Representative for Oregon's 1st district
for.what_they_did: Joined Wyden in introducing the bill.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never acted on the bill after referral; it sat in the Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Self-insured employers and ERISA plans nationally
against.what_they_did: ERISA preemption, the law this bill would have poked a hole in, shields employer plans from state mandates; no group organized around that exemption publicly supported the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Oregon Democrats and the bill drew only one cosponsor, so the record shows no cross-party support and no recorded opposition either.

industries.note: ERISA exempts employer-run plans from state health mandates; the bill would have made Oregon's coverage requirements and assessments apply to them. Employers would bear the cost of mandated coverage.

Insured plans would face Oregon's insurance reforms and the state's high-risk pool, while the employer mandate would push more employers to buy coverage — new customers, under state rules. The bill's uniform-tax condition was written to keep the burden from falling unevenly on insured plans [S3].

Oregon's cost containment and technology assessment laws, which the bill exempts from preemption, would curb provider reimbursement growth, while universal coverage would bring more paying patients into the system [S3].
